rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Real lenses suffer two defects. **Chromatic aberration** comes from dispersion: since n varies with wavelength, the lens maker's formula gives each colour its own focal length — violet (largest n) focuses closest, red farthest — so white-light images show coloured fringes; it vanishes for monochromatic light and is cured by achromatic doublets or by mirrors.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - f ∝ 1/(n − 1) → f_v < f_y < f_r - Marginal focus < paraxial focus (spherical)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Dispersion Definition:** Dispersion is the separation of white light into its constituent colors (spectrum) due to the dependence of the refractive index $n$ on the wavelength $\lambda$ of light ($n(\lambda)$).  ·  **Cauchy's Equation:** For many transparent materials, the refractive index follows Cauchy's equation $n(\lambda) = A + B/\lambda^2 + C/\lambda^4$. This explains why blue light ($\lambda$ smaller) is refracted more than red light ($\lambda$ larger).

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Stopping down does not make glass non-dispersive.  ·  Primary achromatism reduces selected colour separation but may leave secondary spectrum.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Camera lens coatings/edges*** — purple fringing is chromatic aberration; soft corners are spherical.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **Chromatic = colour (dispersion); spherical = geometry (shape)** — two different defects, two different cures.  ·  **Violet focuses closer** (larger n → shorter f); red focuses farther.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Distinguish chromatic from spherical aberration by cause and remedy.  ·  A lens has fv=14.8 cm and fr=15.2 cm. Find Δf.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Answer with cause → effect → remedy for each defect."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Short (2m): Why does a concave mirror have no chromatic aberration?** — Reflection obeys the same law for all wavelengths; no refraction means no dispersion, so all colours focus identically.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **A mirror reflects but never disperses** — reflecting telescopes are colour-free by construction.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Chromatic: n varies with λ → f_v < f_r. Spherical: edge rays focus closer than paraxial rays.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Large astronomical telescopes abandoned objective lenses for mirrors to kill both aberrations at once.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: Spherical aberration remains even for → A  ·  Marginal rays of a convex lens focus → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Why Real Lenses Blur Ideal lenses focus every ray to one point; real lenses don't. Different colours focus at different distances (**chromatic aberration**), and wide beams never meet at a single point (**spherical aberration**). Understanding both defects is the first step to correcting them.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Chromatic aberration - **Cause:** dispersion — n depends on wavelength, so the lens maker's formula gives a different f for each colour: $f_v < f_r$ (violet, larger n, focuses closer). - **Effect:** fringes of colour around white-light images; blurred photographs. - **Nature:** a *chromatic* (colour) defect — absent for monochromatic light.…  ·  ## 3. Conceptual Relationships - **To Topic 80:** chromatic aberration is dispersion applied to a lens (f_v < f_y < f_r). - **To Topic 82:** the achromatic combination cancels chromatic aberration by pairing dispersions. - **To the lens maker's formula:** f ∝ 1/(n − 1) links colour to focus.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Prism Validity:** The formula for dispersive power $\omega = (n_v - n_r)/(n_y - 1)$ assumes small angle of deviation and that the prism is in air. For non-thin prisms or different mediums, angular dispersion depends on the geometry.  ·  No verified PYQ; NEB-style practice (definitions and cures 2–3m).  ·  "Spherical aberration arises because marginal and paraxial rays of the same colour focus at different points."
